title: Knitted-on cast-on
sourceNotes: Technique derived from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 345. Public domain. Dillmont calls this 'knitting on stitches'. Method in wide use in Weldon's Practical Knitting series (1880s onward). Both sources are public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A loop that tightens when the working yarn is pulled, used to anchor the yarn to the needle at the start of a cast-on.
The fundamental knitting action: the needle enters from front to back, yarn wraps around, a new loop is drawn through and the old stitch drops off.
A cast-on worked from a single length of yarn held over thumb and index finger, producing a firm, stretchy edge in one pass.

content.text: The knitted-on cast-on works by turning each new loop into the next stitch. You knit into the needle, pull a loop through, and move it back to the left needle. The cast-on edge is made from knit stitches, so it stretches with the fabric rather than pulling tight.
You need a small ball of yarn and a pair of needles suitable for that yarn weight. A slip knot on the left needle gives you the first stitch to work into.

attrs.alt: Knitting on stitches (the modern knitted-on cast-on)
attrs.title: Fig. 345, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Make a
slip knot
and place it on the left needle. This counts as your first stitch.
Insert the right needle into the slip knot from front to back, as if to
knit
Wrap the yarn around the right needle and draw a new loop through the stitch.
Transfer this new loop onto the left needle by inserting the left needle into the front of the loop from right to left, then sliding the right needle out.
You now have two stitches on the left needle. Repeat steps 2 to 4, always working into the last stitch made, until you have the required number of stitches.
Turn the work. The row of loops sitting on the left needle is your cast-on. Begin the first row of your pattern.
Where you'll see it

Use this cast-on at the start of a project or mid-row when a pattern asks you to add stitches. It works well for button-band extensions or thumb gussets worked flat. Patterns that want a neat, stretchy start often call for it when they do not specify a
long-tail cast-on
Common faults

Twisted stitches on the first row. If you transfer the new loop onto the left needle with the leading leg at the back rather than the front, the stitch sits twisted. Check that the right leg of each new loop faces forward before you begin the first working row.
A loose, loopy cast-on edge. Working into the stitch too loosely leaves gaps. Snug the yarn gently after each transfer without pulling the loop off the needle.
Stitch count creep. Working twice into the same stitch (rather than always into the last stitch just added) adds extra stitches. Count after every five or ten stitches while you build the habit.
What to try next: once this cast-on is comfortable, try the
long-tail cast-on
, which sets up a firmer, more elastic edge in a single pass.
